back: A polymer that can be heated and reshaped many times and can be recycled.
A polymer that is formed once and cannot be reheated, remoulded or recycled.
When first heated and set, a chemical change forms permanent cross-links between the molecule chains. Thermoforming polymers have no cross-links, so their chains slide when heated.
Hard, weather resistant, scratches easily, can be brittle — car headlights, visors, baths, signs.
Lightweight, strong, tough, good heat and chemical resistance — patio chairs, toys, food wrapping film.
Low cost, flexible or rigid, strong and weather resistant — window frames, guttering, cladding.
High density polythene — stiff, lightweight, excellent chemical resistance — buckets, bottles, pipes, washing-up bowls.
Low density polythene — flexible, tough, low cost — carrier bags, squeezy bottles, cling film.
Inexpensive, opaque colours or transparent — vacuum forming in schools and packaging.
Lightweight white beaded foam, excellent insulator, absorbs shock — protective packaging, disposable cups.
Transparent and extremely tough and impact resistant, far tougher than acrylic — safety glasses, riot shields.
Tough, self-lubricating, resists wear — gears, bearings and clothing.
Strong, tough, impact resistant — electronics casings, helmets, LEGO.
Thermoset; resists heat, moisture, scratching and staining — kitchen worktops, tableware.
Thermoset; two-part (resin + hardener), very strong adhesive — adhesives, casting, composites.
Thermoset; hard, stiff, excellent electrical insulator — switches, plugs, electrical fittings.
Thermoset; two-part (resin + catalyst), hard and stiff when set — GRP boat hulls and car body panels, casting.
Synthetic polymers are made from crude oil; natural polymers come from materials like silk, wool, cellulose and proteins.
Pellets, granules and powder; foams, films and filaments; sheets, rods and bars.
